blurb: Letting an AI look things up before it answers: how documents get searched, ranked and quoted — and where it goes wrong.

steps.h: Models stop learning on a date
steps.p: A model only knows what was in its training data, collected up to a date called its knowledge cutoff. It knows nothing after that, and nothing about your private files.
steps.analogy: A brilliant friend who has been on a remote island since last year, with none of your company's documents.

steps.p: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) searches a collection of documents for passages related to your question, then pastes the best ones into the prompt.
The model is told to answer from those passages and say where each point came from, so you can check it.
steps.analogy: An open-book exam instead of one from memory.

steps.p: Change a document and the next answer uses the new version. No retraining needed — the model itself never changes.
If search finds the wrong passages, or the model misreads the right ones, you still get wrong answers — just with a reassuring-looking citation.

cards.q: For answering questions about your company's documents, RAG's main advantage over fine-tuning is that…
options: Documents can be updated instantly and answers can cite sources, with no retraining
It makes the model permanently smarter
cards.hint: What happens when a document changes?
cards.why: Fresh and checkable. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into parameters, which is slow to update and hard to trace. RAG keeps knowledge in documents you can edit and cite.

cards.statement: RAG updates the model's parameters with the documents it retrieves.
cards.why: False. The documents are only pasted into the prompt for that one answer. The model itself is unchanged.

options: The date after which events are missing from its training data
The longest answer it can write
The point where it stops reading a prompt
cards.why: The end of its reading. Anything after that date — news, prices, new products — is unknown to it unless supplied, for example by RAG or web search.

cards.title: The term "retrieval-augmented generation" comes from a 2020 Facebook AI paper.
cards.detail: Patrick Lewis and colleagues coined it. Lewis later joked they'd have picked a nicer name had they known how widely it would be used.

cards.hint: Two things can still go wrong — look at step 5.
cards.why: False. It reduces them for questions the documents answer. But retrieval can miss, and the model can still misread or embellish what it's given.

steps.p: Long documents are split into passages of a few hundred words. Search returns chunks, not whole files, so only the useful part goes in the prompt.

visual.caption: One long document becomes many searchable pieces.

steps.h: Not too big, not too small
steps.p: Tiny chunks lose their context ("it rose 4%" — what did?). Huge chunks bury the answer in noise. Neighbouring chunks often overlap a little so ideas aren't cut in half.
steps.analogy: Cutting a cake: crumbs are useless, and you can't serve the whole cake as one slice.

steps.p: Each chunk is turned into an embedding — a list of numbers capturing its meaning. Chunks about similar things get similar numbers, even with different words.
steps.analogy: Giving every passage a map location; passages about holidays end up in the same neighbourhood.

steps.p: Your question gets an embedding too. The system finds chunks whose numbers are closest to it — the nearest neighbours on the map.
Good systems combine meaning search with old-fashioned keyword search, because each catches what the other misses.

cards.q: What's the main problem with chunks that are too small?
options: They lose surrounding context, so a passage may not make sense alone
They take too long to read
They can't be turned into embeddings
cards.why: Lost context. A tiny chunk may say "it rose 4%" without saying what "it" is. Retrieval then finds it but the model can't use it.

cards.q: Why do many systems let neighbouring chunks overlap a little?
options: So ideas that span a boundary aren't cut in half
To make search slower and more careful
cards.why: Nothing falls through the cracks. An explanation that starts at the end of one chunk is still whole in the next.

cards.statement: Meaning search can find a passage about "getting your money back" when you search for "refund".
cards.why: True. Their embeddings land close together because they mean similar things. Keyword search alone would miss it.

cards.title: Adding one sentence of context to each chunk before searching cut retrieval failures by about half in Anthropic's tests.
cards.detail: Its 2024 "contextual retrieval" had a model write a short note saying where each chunk sits in its document. Combined with keyword search, failed retrievals dropped by roughly half.

cards.statement: You must have a special vector database to build RAG.
cards.why: False. For small collections a simple list in memory works fine, and many ordinary databases now support embeddings. Specialised ones help at large scale.

cards.q: Classic keyword search (BM25) ranks a passage higher when it…
options: Contains your search words, especially rare ones, several times
cards.why: Matching words, rare ones count more. Matching "photosynthesis" says far more than matching "the". It's decades old and still hard to beat for exact terms.

steps.p: Meaning and keyword search quickly pull, say, the top 100 candidate chunks out of millions. Fast, but a bit rough.
A reranker — a model that reads your question and each candidate together — scores how well each one really answers it.
steps.analogy: A recruiter skims 1,000 job applications for keywords; a manager then reads the best 50 properly.

steps.p: Only the top handful go into the prompt. Fewer, better passages mean less noise and lower cost.
Teams check how often the right passage is in the top results. If retrieval misses, no model can answer correctly.
Finally they check whether answers are correct and actually supported by the cited passages — not just plausible.

cards.q: Why is a reranker more accurate than the first search?
options: It reads the question and passage together, comparing them word by word
It searches the web as well
cards.hint: The manager reads the applications properly.
cards.why: It reads them side by side. First-pass search compares two pre-made summaries (embeddings). A reranker reads both texts together, catching details like negation.

cards.statement: Rerankers are usually too slow to run over an entire document collection.
cards.why: True. Reading every chunk alongside each question would take far too long. That's why they only score the first pass's shortlist.

options: How often a relevant passage appears in the top 10 results
How many answers are 10 words long
cards.why: Did the right passage make the top 10? If it's not retrieved, the model never sees it, however clever it is.

cards.statement: When a RAG system gives a wrong answer, the language model is usually to blame.
cards.why: False. Retrieval is a frequent culprit: the right passage was never found, or was split badly. Teams check retrieval before blaming the model.

cards.title: A good answer must be both correct and supported.
cards.detail: Evaluations check "faithfulness": is every claim actually backed by the cited passage? An answer can be true yet unsupported — a sign the model used memory instead of the sources.

cards.title: Check the citation, not just the answer
cards.body: AI search tools can cite a real source that doesn't actually say what the answer claims.
cards.challenge: Next time an AI gives you a cited answer, open one citation and find the exact sentence that supports it.

cards.title: Smarter ways to look things up

steps.p: Instead of one search, an agent can decide what to look up, read results, and search again — like a person following leads.
Users ask vaguely. The system can rewrite the question into several clearer searches first, which finds more of what's relevant.
A trick called HyDE has the model write a hypothetical answer, then searches for passages similar to that — answers look more like answers than questions do.
steps.analogy: Looking for a lost photo by describing what's in it, rather than describing why you want it.

steps.p: GraphRAG builds a map of people, places and themes across all documents, so it can answer big-picture questions like "What are the main themes here?"
Anything retrieved goes into the prompt — including hidden instructions planted in a document. That's prompt injection, arriving through search.

cards.q: GraphRAG was designed for questions like…
options: "What are the main themes across all these documents?"
cards.why: Big-picture questions. Ordinary RAG fetches a few passages, which can't summarise a whole collection. A map of connections can.

cards.q: HyDE improves search by looking for passages similar to…
options: A hypothetical answer the model writes first
cards.why: A guessed answer. Even if the guess is partly wrong, it's shaped like the passage you want, so its embedding lands near the real answer.

cards.statement: Now that models can read a million tokens at once, RAG is obsolete.
cards.why: False. Most collections are far bigger than a million tokens, and stuffing everything in costs more, runs slower and can hurt accuracy. Retrieval still narrows things down.

cards.title: A single planted document can hijack an AI assistant that searches.
cards.detail: Researchers (Greshake et al., 2023) showed that text with hidden instructions, once retrieved into a prompt, can steer an assistant — for example, making it push a scam link.

cards.statement: A question and its correct answer always have very similar embeddings.
cards.why: False. A question and its answer can be worded very differently. That gap is exactly what HyDE and rerankers try to bridge.
